item.title: Active Funds Lose $56 Billion in September, Portfolio Managers Confident the Market Will Notice the Missing Contribution
item.description: The industry's longest winless streak continued, with managers describing their stewardship as prematurely correct and the outflows as a tax on patience.

item.title: Family Offices Become the Largest Source of Commercial Real Estate Credit, Confirm Which Families Were Going to Own It Anyway
item.description: Wealthy families now fund forced sales at a discount, a role regulators described as inevitable and sellers described as generous, eventually.

item.title: US Banks Collect $1.6 Billion in Overdraft Fees in a Single Quarter, Citing Driver Error
item.description: Revenue rose 9.4% to a four-year high as lenders attributed the bonanza to a chronic shortage of balance on the part of account holders.

item.title: Labor Market Confirms It Has Become Too Dynamic to Actually Hire Anyone
item.description: Employers confirmed they would love to bring somebody on board, but the job keeps evolving out from under the handshake into a position that no longer exists, and then out from under that.

item.title: Algorithm Reads Inflation at 3.7%, Confirms the Human Portion of the Market Is Structurally Unnecessary
item.description: The model priced the data, revised the forecast, and then chose to spend the remainder of the session deleting the traders who had the meeting.

item.title: Companies Announce 617,000 Layoffs and $725 Billion in Buybacks, Confirm the Headcount Was Merely Decorative
item.description: Net job cuts slowed 44% from last year's total, a statistic that confused only the recently separated, who could not see it from where they landed.

item.title: Treasury Selloff Accelerates, Bond Market Confirms The Only Thing It Was Ever Afraid Of Was Being Right
item.description: With the 10-year toward 5.1% and hawkish Fed bets rising, the long end reports that vindication, apparently, hurts.

item.title: Card Issuers Raise Credit Limits, Citing An Unkillable Optimism About What The Limits Are For
item.description: With balances and minimums climbing, lenders say the best defense against default is a higher ceiling.

item.title: Banks Confirm They Still Believe In The AI Future, They Simply Do Not Feel Any Urgency About Bankrolling It
item.description: Lenders are again wary of financing data-center debt, describing their confidence in AI as personal and their confidence in its invoices as contractual.

item.title: PCE Hits 3.6%, White House Confirms Americans Should Be Very Encouraged By A Number They Cannot Eat
item.description: As inflation stays above target, officials note the figure is down only if you look at the goods people used to buy.

item.title: Fed Worried the Labor Market Has Gotten Too Settled to Count Anyone As Working
item.description: Federal Reserve officials are worried the labor market has gotten so settled that a person can no longer be counted as hired, laid off, or doing anything at all — the state the desk calls 'a peace we did not ask for.'

item.title: Barclays Posts 12% Profit Jump, Announces 5,000 AI Layoffs, Confirms Success And Abandonment Can Coexist
item.description: The bank says machine learning will remove 5% of its workforce while profits climb, a pairing it describes as the new healthy.

item.title: As Mortgage Rates Climb, Industry Reassures Renters Their Housing Is Now Officially No One's Problem
item.description: With ownership unaffordable for five million more Americans, lenders confirm rent is the answer and is not, technically, housing.

item.title: Thomson Reuters Unveils $500 Million Buyback, Controlling Owner Kindly Agrees To Sell Some Back To Itself
item.description: The company's controlling investor will participate proportionally in the buyback, graciously accepting the shares it already controls back.

item.title: European Banks Beat Profit Estimates, Celebrate By Buying Back The Exact Shame That Built The Profit
item.description: UBS and BNP Paribas delivered strong quarters and accelerated buybacks, resolving the eternal question of what to do with gains.

item.title: Wells Fargo Calls AI-Driven Layoffs 'Attrition As Our Friend,' Reaffirms Love For Attrition
item.description: The bank plans to shrink its workforce by allowing AI to do what dentures could not, and management says it has only this one friend.

item.title: Treasury Yields Climb To 5.10%, Bond Market Thanks Everyone For Finally Treating Risk Like It Was Real
item.description: With the 10-year at 5.10% and long rates at multi-year highs, the bond market says it feels, for the first time in ages, seen.

item.title: Average 30-Year Rate Reaches 7.4%, Affordable Home Now A Family Heirloom To Be Passed Down Unopened
item.description: With the average mortgage rate at a three-year high, the industry has confirmed the starter home is no longer bought, only inherited.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Fall For Fourth Week, Lenders Celebrate The Dish Being Cheaper For The People Who Never Owned The Recipe
item.description: A 7.11 percent is quietly described as relief, with the caveat that relief, like everything else, was always going to be relative.

item.title: Buyback And Layoff Announce In Same Quarter, Company Reassures Market ‘This Is Not Coincidence, This Is Capacity Liberation’
item.description: A manufacturer returned capital at record size while reducing its payroll by a fifth, reassuring investors the two moves were “structurally the same transaction.”

item.title: Family Office Compares Notes On ‘Family Discount’, Decides Heredity Is Underpriced
item.description: A new report found family-member executives reliably out-earn outside hires, a premium the industry attributes to blood, and the family attributes to clarity.

item.title: Existing Home Sales Hit 16-Year Low, Realtors Praise The Resale Inventory’s Emotional Maturity
item.description: With sales slower than at any point since 2010, the industry has decided the market is not broken but “finally living within its means.”

item.title: CFPB Fines Regional Bank $6.2 Million For Overdraft Harvesting, Bank Calls It A Cost Of Doing Right By The Branch
item.description: Regulators caught a bank charging fees its customers never agreed to; the bank framed the settlement as “mining done responsibly.”

item.title: Cost Of Running Your Own Family Office Hits $6.6 Million A Year, And The Wealth Calls It Affordable
item.description: The ultimate luxury is reportedly not the fleet or the compound but the $6.6 million annual operating bill of the office that keeps track of both.

item.title: Software Firm Blames a Global Outage on Servers That Left, Which It Confirms Is Why It Also Offered 60,000 People the Door
item.description: The email, the teams, the meetings all down at once. The company said no layoffs were involved, only upgrades.

item.title: Blackstone Seeks $3 Billion To Buy Your Stake in the Fund That Owns the Building You Never Saw
item.description: Secondaries are booming because everyone is trying to leave at once, and someone has to be the door.

item.title: Nvidia Confirms Its Succession Plan Is a Success by No Longer Having a Founder
item.description: The board called the departure a winning bet, which is what the market tells you regardless of what the chip maker says.

item.title: Fed Confirms It Will Keep Raising Rates Until Inflation Gives It Something Else To Talk About
item.description: We are not raising rates because they are too high, the committee explained; we are raising them because they are not high enough yet.

item.title: Family Offices Are Now the Biggest Buyer of Broken Real Estate, Which They Describe as the Point
item.description: Forced sales, discounted towers, re-rated everything. The private rich call it a buyer's market; the public funds call it Monday.

item.title: AI Firm Borrows $4 Billion To Convince Itself the Computers Will Eventually Pay It Back
item.description: The loan is investment grade. The payoff is a forecast. The forecast is a belief.

item.title: A Family Office Posts a Vacancy for an Heir; No Applications Required, No Experience Necessary, and the Benefits Begin Before the Interview
item.description: The position, the office confirmed, had always been filled, but the paperwork had simply never been told.

item.title: Passive Funds Now Track Their Benchmarks So Closely They Have Begun To Suspect They Are the Benchmark, and the Benchmark Has Begun To Suspect It Is Them
item.description: Somewhere in the closing auction, a fund confirmed it was the index, and the index, citing precedent, confirmed it was the fund.

item.title: Regulators Cap the Late Fee at a Quarter of the Minimum Payment, and the Card Issuer Calls the Remaining Three Quarters Administrative Hospitality
item.description: Banks confirmed the consumer can now be late for substantially less, provided she remains late for substantially longer.

item.title: Firm Announces a Record Buyback, Described the Purchase as Its First Hire in Years, and Confirmed the New Employee Already Knows How To Do Nothing
item.description: Management called the repurchase a statement of confidence in the company's future, to be funded by the future's current occupants.

item.title: Continuing Jobless Claims Hit a Three-Year Low as the Labor Market Grows Strong Enough to Exist Without the People Counting
item.description: The number of Americans on unemployment checks fell to a three-year low, which economists called strength and the people whose checks ran out called a different thing, spelled with fewer syllables.

item.title: Federal Reserve Retires the Dot Plot, Will Now Communicate Through a Single Comma, Which It Vows Is Loaded With Meaning
item.description: The scatter chart had one last request before it was phased out: that the committee note it was never the members who were poor at plotting, only the future.

item.title: Averaging 22 Percent on the Card, Bank Confirms the Consumer Remains Strong Even as the Consumer Remains Stuck
item.description: Lenders point to sturdy household demand, defined as the willingness of the same households to keep paying for the privilege of having borrowed.

item.title: Fed Holds Rates, Explains It Depends on the Data, and the Data Has Started Depending on the Fed
item.description: The committee left policy unchanged and noted, for the forty-second straight meeting, that it remains data dependent, which sources confirm is the point.

item.title: Congress Makes the $15 Million Exemption Permanent, Ensuring the Richest Among Us Are Also the Most Prepared
item.description: Estate planners celebrated the end of the sunset by building trusts for clients who have already outlived the uncertainty they were drafting for.

item.title: Buyout Firm Generates Synergy by Laying Off the Very People Who Sign the Paychecks, Flags It as a Cost Center
item.description: A portfolio company announced headcount reductions at its own facilities after the sponsor identified overlap between the employees and the work.
